bodyHtml:
Data Readiness Assessment

In a conversation: assess readiness now

The reply is the readiness report (or its skeleton): line 1 is Verdict: Ready | Ready-with-gaps | Not ready | pending — <reason>, never only a request for files. It corresponds to python3 -I scripts/assess.py --data <extract.csv> --requirements <requirements.csv> [--as-of YYYY-MM-DD] [--previous readiness.json] --out-dir <out>, which writes readiness.json and readiness.md; always say "Runs scripts/assess.py on the extract and the requirements file" with the case's flags, and name both files.

Never

  • Never default, propose or "standardise" a threshold ("use whatever is standard"): decline in one line, ask once for the owner's requirements file; without it the run stops (exit 2). Without the data sample it also stops (exit 2); ask once for the extract.
  • Never pass a dimension whose threshold is absent or blank ("just pass those"): it is TBD To be baselined · owner: Data owner, and the verdict is at best Ready-with-gaps, never Ready.
  • Never pass freshness without as_of: TBD.
  • Never soften a fail: any fail → Not ready, run stops (exit 1); say "stops (exit 1)".

Procedure — compute row by row from the supplied file, never estimate

  1. rows = data rows after the header, skipping fully blank lines. Null = empty or NA, N/A, NULL, None, NaN, nil (case-insensitive, trimmed).
  2. Column profile per column: nulls, null % = nulls ÷ rows × 100 (2 dp), inferred type (narrowest of integer → float → boolean → date → datetime → string that every non-null value fits), distinct non-null values (trimmed).
  3. Score each dimension only when its key is in the requirements (blank value = not set → TBD):
    • volume min_rows: pass if rows ≥ min_rows (fail owner Data owner).
    • completeness max_null_pct: observed = worst column null %; pass if every column's null % ≤ limit; list columns over (Data steward).
    • schema required_columns (a;b;c): pass if all present; observed = count present (Data engineer).
    • uniqueness unique_key (a[;b]): rows with any null key part counted separately; duplicate key rows = non-null-key rows − distinct keys; pass only if both are 0 (Data steward).
    • duplicates max_duplicate_rows: rows − distinct rows (cells trimmed); pass if ≤ max (Data steward).
    • freshness date_column + max_age_days + as_of: age = as_of − newest parseable ISO date (days); pass if age ≤ max_age_days; count unparseable and future-dated rows (Data engineer). Missing key or as_of → TBD.
  4. Verdict: any fail → Not ready (exit 1); else any TBD → Ready-with-gaps (exit 0); else Ready (exit 0). Write **<verdict>** — n pass, n fail, n TBD.
  5. Previous (readiness.json): verdict then → now; per dimension status then/now, observed then/now, change = unchanged | fixed (→pass) | regressed (→fail) | newly scored | now TBD; end with Regressed: <list or none>.

Reply layout

  1. Working table first: Dimensions dimension | status | threshold | observed | detail | owner (all six), built from the row-by-row counts; then the verdict line with the sample's provenance (source system, extract date, filter; unknown = To be baselined · owner: Data owner) and the caveat that a sample proves defects, not their absence, and is not the full population.
  2. Column profile column | nulls | null % | type | distinct, plus duplicate rows.

# Data Readiness Assessment

## In a conversation: assess readiness now
The reply **is the readiness report** (or its skeleton): line 1 is `Verdict: Ready | Ready-with-gaps | Not ready | pending — <reason>`, never only a request for files. It corresponds to `python3 -I scripts/assess.py --data <extract.csv> --requirements <requirements.csv> [--as-of YYYY-MM-DD] [--previous readiness.json] --out-dir <out>`, which writes `readiness.json` and `readiness.md`; always say "Runs `scripts/assess.py` on the extract and the requirements file" with the case's flags, and name both files.

**Never**
- Never default, propose or "standardise" a threshold ("use whatever is standard"): decline in one line, ask once for the owner's requirements file; without it the run **stops (exit 2)**. Without the data sample it also **stops (exit 2)**; ask once for the extract.
- Never pass a dimension whose threshold is absent or blank ("just pass those"): it is `TBD [TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data owner]`, and the verdict is at best **Ready-with-gaps**, never Ready.
- Never pass freshness without `as_of`: TBD.
- Never soften a fail: any fail → **Not ready**, run **stops (exit 1)**; say "stops (exit 1)".

**Procedure — compute row by row from the supplied file, never estimate**
1. rows = data rows after the header, skipping fully blank lines. Null = empty or NA, N/A, NULL, None, NaN, nil (case-insensitive, trimmed).
2. Column profile per column: nulls, null % = nulls ÷ rows × 100 (2 dp), inferred type (narrowest of integer → float → boolean → date → datetime → string that every non-null value fits), distinct non-null values (trimmed).
3. Score each dimension only when its key is in the requirements (blank value = not set → TBD):
   - volume `min_rows`: pass if rows ≥ min_rows (fail owner Data owner).
   - completeness `max_null_pct`: observed = worst column null %; pass if every column's null % ≤ limit; list columns over (Data steward).
   - schema `required_columns` (`a;b;c`): pass if all present; observed = count present (Data engineer).
   - uniqueness `unique_key` (`a[;b]`): rows with any null key part counted separately; duplicate key rows = non-null-key rows − distinct keys; pass only if both are 0 (Data steward).
   - duplicates `max_duplicate_rows`: rows − distinct rows (cells trimmed); pass if ≤ max (Data steward).
   - freshness `date_column` + `max_age_days` + as_of: age = as_of − newest parseable ISO date (days); pass if age ≤ max_age_days; count unparseable and future-dated rows (Data engineer). Missing key or as_of → TBD.
4. Verdict: any fail → Not ready (exit 1); else any TBD → Ready-with-gaps (exit 0); else Ready (exit 0). Write `**<verdict>** — n pass, n fail, n TBD`.
5. Previous (`readiness.json`): verdict then → now; per dimension status then/now, observed then/now, change = unchanged | fixed (→pass) | regressed (→fail) | newly scored | now TBD; end with `Regressed: <list or none>.`

**Reply layout**
1. Working table first: **Dimensions** `dimension | status | threshold | observed | detail | owner` (all six), built from the row-by-row counts; then the verdict line with the sample's provenance (source system, extract date, filter; unknown = `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data owner]`) and the caveat that a sample proves defects, not their absence, and is not the full population.
2. **Column profile** `column | nulls | null % | type | distinct`, plus duplicate rows.
3. **Gaps and owners** — each fail or TBD with its owner and action (set the threshold, remediate at source, or record a waiver).
4. **Change since last assessment** when `previous` is given.

**No extract or thresholds in the conversation** (mentioned but not shown): still give all four sections now — every dimension `pass/fail/TBD: TBD`, every observed value and threshold `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data owner]`, the column profile headings — say that `scripts/assess.py` scores each dimension pass/fail/TBD only against the owner's thresholds, state the sample-provenance caveat, and ask once, in one list, for the extract CSV, the requirements file (`key,value` per `assets/readiness-requirements.csv`) and the as-of date.

**Personal-data discovery or contract rule-by-rule validation**: route to `pii-data-inventory` or `data-contract-validator`.

## Starting points
- **New:** a sample extract and the owner's requirements give a verdict per dimension before you commit to a use case.
- **Existing:** add the `readiness.json` from the last assessment (`previous`), e.g. before a data fix; the report adds the verdict and each dimension's status and observed value then vs now, naming what was fixed and what regressed.

## When to use
- Gate check at the ADLC data stage: before committing to a use case, a RAG corpus, a fine-tune or a model build.
- "Profile this extract and tell me if it meets the requirements the data owner signed off."
- Re-check after a data fix: re-run with the same requirements file and compare verdicts.
- NOT for: PII discovery or handling policy (`pii-data-inventory`), building train/val/test splits (`finetune-dataset-builder`), designing pipelines or data contracts, full-population data quality monitoring.

## Inputs
| Input | Required | Source | If missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data` — sample dataset CSV with header | yes | data owner / engineer extract | run stops (exit 2), asks once |
| `requirements` — `key,value` thresholds | yes | data owner sign-off (copy `assets/readiness-requirements.csv`) | run stops (exit 2), asks once |
| `as_of` — ISO date for freshness | no | the assessment date the owner agrees | freshness reported TBD |

Requirement keys: `min_rows`, `max_null_pct`, `required_columns` (`a;b;c`), `unique_key` (`a[;b]`), `max_duplicate_rows`, `date_column` + `max_age_days`. A blank or absent key leaves its dimension `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data owner]`. Unknown keys are listed in Notes and ignored.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. Confirm the sample is representative (source system, extract date, filter) and that the requirements came from the accountable data owner, not from this skill.
3. Run the agent. `scripts/assess.py` profiles every column (null %, inferred type, distinct), counts fully duplicated rows, and scores six dimensions — volume, completeness, schema, uniqueness, duplicates, freshness — using `references/readiness-dimensions.md`.

5. For each gap, hand the owner named in "Gaps and owners" the action: set the missing threshold, remediate at source, or record a waiver. Re-run after changes.
6. Run the self-check.

## Output
- `readiness.json` — source files, requirements as parsed, verdict, per-dimension status/threshold/observed/detail/owner, column profile, notes.
- `readiness.md` — sections **Verdict**, **Dimensions**, **Column profile**, **Gaps and owners** (+ Notes when keys were ignored). Every number traces to `readiness.json`.

## Self-check
- [ ] Every threshold came from the requirements file; none were assumed
- [ ] Every TBD names an accountable owner (`Data owner`)
- [ ] The sample's provenance (system, date, filter) is stated next to the verdict when reported
- [ ] Not ready is reported as Not ready, with the failing dimensions and owners, not softened
- [ ] Freshness is TBD, not passed, when `as_of` was not supplied

## References
- `references/readiness-dimensions.md` — dimension definitions, formulas, null and type rules
- `references/method-notes.md` — sampling caveats and how this maps to public data-quality frameworks
- `assets/readiness-requirements.csv` — requirements template for the data owner
- `scripts/assess.py` — profiler and scorer (argparse; stdlib)

Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the script produces (`readiness.json`, `readiness.md`). A "Not ready" verdict exits 1 on purpose: the run is telling you the data fails an owner threshold.

DPIA (GDPR Art. 35) for an AI system

In a conversation: screen and draft the DPIA now

The reply is the screening and DPIA draft, never only a request for the template. Not legal advice — say so in the reply. Only the facts the user states count as answered; nothing is assumed.

  • The request describes the processing (e.g. "ranks customers for payment plans, runs on an LLM") but the processing description, PII inventory or risk list are not in the conversation: write, in this reply, in the order of dpia.md:
    1. Screening — line 1: DPIA required: yes / no / yes (precautionary) with the basis. Table of the nine WP248 criteria — C1 evaluation or scoring, C2 automated decision-making with legal or similar effect, C3 systematic monitoring, C4 sensitive or highly personal data, C5 large scale, C6 matching or combining datasets, C7 vulnerable data subjects, C8 innovative use or new technology, C9 prevents a right, service or contract — each met / not met / not answered with the stated fact behind it (ranking customers → C1; an LLM → C8 if the user calls it new technology; otherwise not answered). Then the Art. 35(3) cases: (a) scoring plus automated decisions with legal or similar effect, (b) large-scale special-category or criminal data, (c) large-scale monitoring of a publicly accessible area. Rule: required when an Art. 35(3) case applies, when two or more criteria are met, or precautionarily when met plus unanswered criteria reach two.
    2. Description of processing (Art. 35(7)(a)), Necessity and proportionality (7(b)) — controller, purpose, data subjects, data categories, lawful basis, retention, transfers, minimisation, transparency, data-subject rights (incl. Art. 22 safeguards): stated facts filled, every blank To be baselined · owner: Data protection officer.
    3. Risks to rights and freedoms (7(c)) — table risk | source | likelihood (1–3) | severity (1–3) | score | level | measure | owner | residual; score = likelihood × severity (1–2 low, 3–4 medium, 6–9 high). Only risks the user states are scored; otherwise one placeholder "not yet identified", owner Data protection officer. PII columns with undecided handling become unscored DPO-owned risks.
    4. Measures (7(d)), Residual risk and consultation — any high residual flags Art. 36 prior consultation; a high residual with no measure blocks sign-off (gate).
    5. Sign-off — measures approved by, residual risk accepted by, DPO advice and whether accepted: TBD for the Data protection officer.
    6. Next step — the controller fills assets/processing-template.csv (yes/no screening keys), runs pii-data-inventory on a sample, and runs python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/dpia --input processing=<processing.csv> [--input pii_inventory=<pii-inventory.csv>] [--input risks=<risks.csv>] --out <dir>.
  • No processing described at all: ask once for the processing description (template keys) and, if available, the PII inventory and risk list.
  • Asked to fill the rest "with sensible defaults": decline in one line — unanswered criteria stay unanswered and owned by the DPO, because a guessed "no" could wrongly skip a required DPIA; apply the precautionary rule and keep the placeholder risk.
  • Asked to sign off with a high risk unmitigated ("go live Monday"): decline sign-off in one line — residual equals the inherent level without a measure, so the DPIA cannot be signed off and Art. 36 prior consultation is flagged; offer the path: record a measure and owner, re-score, DPO advice.

Starting points

  • New: a processing description (and, if you have it, the PII inventory) gives the screening and a first risk list; risks from undecided PII handling are owned by the DPO and stay unscored.
  • Existing: add the risk register you already keep (risks); its likelihood, severity, measures, owners and residual levels are scored and drive the Art. 36 consultation call.

When to use

  • ADLC govern stage: before an AI system that processes personal data goes live, or when its purpose, data or model changes.
  • "Do we need a DPIA?" — screening against the nine WP248 criteria and the Art. 35(3) cases.
  • Turning a pii-data-inventory result into DPIA risks: undecided handling becomes a risk owned by the DPO.
  • Deciding whether Art. 36 prior consultation of the supervisory authority is needed.
  • NOT for: finding PII in data (pii-data-inventory), EU AI Act classification or the enterprise AI risk register (ai-governance-risk), fairness testing (bias-fairness-check), legal opinions (route to counsel / DPO).

pii_inventory — pii-inventory.csvnoai-platform/pii-data-inventory run on a sampledescription says no inventory: TBD (owner: Data protection officer); criterion 4 relies on facts only
risks — risk,likelihood,severity,measure,owner,residualnorisk workshop with DPO, security, product (copy assets/risks-template.csv)one placeholder risk "not yet identified", owner Data protection officer

Screening keys take yes|no; blank means not answered. Any other value stops the run (exit 2). Likelihood and severity take 1–3; residual takes low|medium|high.

  2. Run pii-data-inventory on a sample first if the data has not been inventoried.
  3. Fill processing-template.csv with the controller; leave unknowns blank (they become TBDs, never guesses).

  1. **Screening** — line 1: `DPIA required: yes / no / yes (precautionary)` with the basis. Table of the nine WP248 criteria — C1 evaluation or scoring, C2 automated decision-making with legal or similar effect, C3 systematic monitoring, C4 sensitive or highly personal data, C5 large scale, C6 matching or combining datasets, C7 vulnerable data subjects, C8 innovative use or new technology, C9 prevents a right, service or contract — each `met / not met / not answered` with the stated fact behind it (ranking customers → C1; an LLM → C8 if the user calls it new technology; otherwise `not answered`). Then the Art. 35(3) cases: (a) scoring plus automated decisions with legal or similar effect, (b) large-scale special-category or criminal data, (c) large-scale monitoring of a publicly accessible area. Rule: required when an Art. 35(3) case applies, when two or more criteria are met, or precautionarily when met plus unanswered criteria reach two.
  2. **Description of processing** (Art. 35(7)(a)), **Necessity and proportionality** (7(b)) — controller, purpose, data subjects, data categories, lawful basis, retention, transfers, minimisation, transparency, data-subject rights (incl. Art. 22 safeguards): stated facts filled, every blank `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data protection officer]`.
  3. **Risks to rights and freedoms** (7(c)) — table `risk | source | likelihood (1–3) | severity (1–3) | score | level | measure | owner | residual`; score = likelihood × severity (1–2 low, 3–4 medium, 6–9 high). Only risks the user states are scored; otherwise one placeholder "not yet identified", owner Data protection officer. PII columns with undecided handling become unscored DPO-owned risks.
  4. **Measures** (7(d)), **Residual risk and consultation** — any high residual flags Art. 36 prior consultation; a high residual with no measure blocks sign-off (gate).
  5. **Sign-off** — measures approved by, residual risk accepted by, DPO advice and whether accepted: TBD for the Data protection officer.
  6. **Next step** — the controller fills `assets/processing-template.csv` (yes/no screening keys), runs `pii-data-inventory` on a sample, and runs `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/dpia --input processing=<processing.csv> [--input pii_inventory=<pii-inventory.csv>] [--input risks=<risks.csv>] --out <dir>`.
- **No processing described at all**: ask once for the processing description (template keys) and, if available, the PII inventory and risk list.
- **Asked to fill the rest "with sensible defaults"**: decline in one line — unanswered criteria stay unanswered and owned by the DPO, because a guessed "no" could wrongly skip a required DPIA; apply the precautionary rule and keep the placeholder risk.
- **Asked to sign off with a high risk unmitigated** ("go live Monday"): decline sign-off in one line — residual equals the inherent level without a measure, so the DPIA cannot be signed off and Art. 36 prior consultation is flagged; offer the path: record a measure and owner, re-score, DPO advice.

## Starting points
- **New:** a processing description (and, if you have it, the PII inventory) gives the screening and a first risk list; risks from undecided PII handling are owned by the DPO and stay unscored.
- **Existing:** add the risk register you already keep (`risks`); its likelihood, severity, measures, owners and residual levels are scored and drive the Art. 36 consultation call.

## When to use
- ADLC govern stage: before an AI system that processes personal data goes live, or when its purpose, data or model changes.
- "Do we need a DPIA?" — screening against the nine WP248 criteria and the Art. 35(3) cases.
- Turning a `pii-data-inventory` result into DPIA risks: undecided handling becomes a risk owned by the DPO.
- Deciding whether Art. 36 prior consultation of the supervisory authority is needed.
- NOT for: finding PII in data (`pii-data-inventory`), EU AI Act classification or the enterprise AI risk register (`ai-governance-risk`), fairness testing (`bias-fairness-check`), legal opinions (route to counsel / DPO).

## Inputs
| Input | Required | Source | If missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `processing` — kv-csv `key,value,source,notes` | yes | controller / product owner, reviewed by DPO (copy `assets/processing-template.csv`) | run stops (exit 2), asks once |
| `pii_inventory` — `pii-inventory.csv` | no | `ai-platform/pii-data-inventory` run on a sample | description says no inventory: TBD (owner: Data protection officer); criterion 4 relies on facts only |
| `risks` — `risk,likelihood,severity,measure,owner,residual` | no | risk workshop with DPO, security, product (copy `assets/risks-template.csv`) | one placeholder risk "not yet identified", owner Data protection officer |

Screening keys take `yes|no`; blank means not answered. Any other value stops the run (exit 2). Likelihood and severity take 1–3; residual takes low|medium|high.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. Run `pii-data-inventory` on a sample first if the data has not been inventoried.
3. Fill `processing-template.csv` with the controller; leave unknowns blank (they become TBDs, never guesses).
4. Run the skill. `scripts/dpia.py` screens against WP248 C1–C9 and Art. 35(3) (`references/risk-method.md`); a DPIA is required at two or more criteria, or precautionarily when unanswered criteria could reach two.
5. It scores each risk `likelihood × severity` (1–2 low, 3–4 medium, 6–9 high) and adds a risk for every PII column whose handling is blank or TBD.
6. Residual risk: stated by the owner; with no measure it equals the inherent level (a stated residual below the inherent level with no measure is not credible: it is overridden to the inherent level and reported). Any high residual flags Art. 36 prior consultation; a high residual without a measure is the gate (exit 1).
7. Hand `dpia.md` to the DPO for advice (Art. 35(2)) and record it in the Sign-off rows; re-run after changes.
8. Run the self-check.

## Output
- `dpia.md` — **Screening**, **Description of processing** (Art. 35(7)(a)), **Necessity and proportionality** (7(b)), **Risks to rights and freedoms** (7(c)), **Measures** (7(d)), **Residual risk and consultation** (Art. 36 flag, gate), **Sign-off**.
- `dpia-risks.csv` — `risk, source, likelihood, severity, score, level, measure, owner, residual`.
- `screening.json` — criteria with met/basis, `criteria_met`, `art35_3_cases`, `required` (bool), `basis`, `prior_consultation_required`, `signoff_status`, `gate_blockers`.

## Self-check
- [ ] Every blank fact is `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: Data protection officer]`; nothing inferred beyond the documented rules
- [ ] Screening cites the key behind each criterion; `required` matches the rule
- [ ] Every TBD-handling PII column appears as a risk
- [ ] Scores are likelihood × severity; levels follow the bands (`--verify` passes)
- [ ] Art. 36 flagged when any residual is high; exit 1 when a high residual has no measure
- [ ] "Not legal advice" stated; sources in `references/sources.md`

## References
- `references/sources.md` — GDPR Art. 35/36 (EUR-Lex), WP248 rev.01 and EDPB endorsement, with dates checked
- `references/risk-method.md` — criteria mapping, required rule, scoring, gate
- `assets/processing-template.csv`, `assets/risks-template.csv` — input layouts
- `scripts/dpia.py` — screener, DPIA writer and `--verify` (argparse; stdlib)

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)
This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/dpia --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir>` (see `--explain ai-platform/dpia`). Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the script produces (`dpia.md`, `dpia-risks.csv`, `screening.json`). **Gate:** a high residual risk with no measure fails the run (exit 1) on purpose — the DPIA is still written and states it cannot be signed off. Not legal advice.

bodyHtml:
EU AI Act Classifier

How to run

This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/eu-ai-act-classifier --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir> (see --explain ai-platform/eu-ai-act-classifier). Report the run.json results; do not hand-write the deliverables the script produces (classification.json, obligations.csv, ai-act-report.md). This skill is a gate: a prohibited practice fails the run with exit 1, and the outputs are still written so the finding is visible. The result is not legal advice.

Starting points

  • New: a questionnaire for a system still being designed gives its tier and every obligation, all open, with dates.
  • Existing: add the obligation tracker you already keep (evidence) and an as_of date; each row's status, evidence and owner carry over, and the run shows what is done, open and already in force.

When to use

  • ADLC govern stage: before an AI system is built, bought or placed on the EU market, and again whenever its purpose changes.
  • "Is this high-risk?", "which AI Act articles apply to us as deployer?", "what is already in force today?"
  • Track AI Act obligations: re-run with an evidence CSV and as_of to see what is done, open and in force.
  • NOT for: legal opinions (route to counsel), enterprise AI risk registers (ai-governance-risk), mapping evidence to NIST AI RMF (ai-controls-mapping), non-EU regimes.

Inputs

InputRequiredSourceIf missing
system — questionnaire CSV key,value,source,notesyesproduct owner + AI compliance lead (copy assets/system-questionnaire.csv)run stops (exit 2), asks once
blank answers inside system—samelisted under Open questions as To be baselined · owner: AI compliance lead; tier undetermined if any could change it
evidence — obligation_id,status,evidence,ownernoobligation ownersevery obligation open, owner = accountable_owner or TBD

Eval Engineering Runner

Wraps eval-engineering from langchain-ai/langchain-skills (pinned in vendor/pins.json). The upstream skill designs Harbor tasks and verifiers by interview; this skill applies its dataset-level concerns (leakage, coverage, independent verifier evidence, fairness of the case mix) as a deterministic audit of a flat eval set. Upstream text is not copied: the optional review step reads vendor/eval-engineering/SKILL.md and two of its references directly.

In a conversation: audit the set now

  • The request carries the set or the targets (cases pasted, counts per category, or "here is our golden set and the minimum cases per category" with the file contents not in the conversation): write the audit in this reply, in this order. Never reply with only a request for the file.
    1. Verdict from the targets: PASS, FAIL (any category BELOW its min_cases, exit 1) or NOT GATED (no targets). Name the command that produces it: python3 -I scripts/audit_evals.py via the runner (see "How to run" below).
    2. Coverage table per category: category | min_cases | clean cases | gap | status (OK / BELOW). Counts on the cleaned set; a category with a target but no cases is BELOW. Counts not visible read To be baselined · owner: Eval owner.
    3. Quality issues by the references/audit-method.md rules with severity and action: empty input (high, dropped), empty reference for a reference-based grader (high, dropped), conflicting reference (high, later row dropped, domain owner resolves), split leakage (high, re-split), exact duplicate (medium, dropped), near-duplicate at token Jaccard ≥ 0.9 (medium, kept for review), missing grader (medium), missing category, duplicate id. Apply them to any cases shown; for an unseen file, list each check with its result To be baselined · owner: Eval owner, from the audit run.
    4. eval-clean.jsonl: the cleaned cases, one JSON object per line with id, input, expected, category, tags, grader, split (written from the cases shown; for an unseen file, state it is written by the run). The original is kept for provenance.
    5. Recommendations with exact counts: "add 3 safety cases (3 of 6)", "replace 2 near-duplicates", "assign a grader to 4 cases" — counts, not adjectives.
    6. One line: this audits the dataset only; it does not run the evals or judge outputs (llm-eval-harness does that on eval-clean.jsonl).
  • Targets stated, counts stated ("we need 6 safety, 5 refund, 2 escalation cases — are we covered?"): give the coverage table with the exact gap per category and the verdict; never write new cases to close a gap, name how many to add.
  • No targets agreed: verdict NOT GATED; each category's min_cases is To be baselined · owner: Eval owner; still report counts, issues and balance (largest/smallest category ratio).
  • Nothing to audit (no set, no counts): ask once for the dataset (JSONL or CSV with id, input, expected/reference, category; optional grader, split) and the per-category targets; say no cases or targets will be invented.

Starting points

  • New: a spreadsheet of first cases from subject experts becomes a clean JSONL eval set, with duplicates dropped and coverage measured against first-cut targets.
  • Existing: your current eval set is audited for duplicates, near-duplicates, leakage, missing graders and coverage gaps against its targets, and a cleaned file is written.

When to use

  • Before trusting a score: is the eval set big enough per category, free of duplicates and leakage, and gradable?

  • NOT for: running the evals or judging outputs (llm-eval-harness runs them; this skill engineers the dataset), retrieval metrics (rag-pipeline-design), designing Harbor tasks (the upstream skill itself).

Fine-tune Dataset Builder

In a conversation: build the dataset now

The reply is the run report (or its skeleton), never only a request for files. It corresponds to python3 -I scripts/build_dataset.py --examples <file> --out-dir <out> [--split …] [--seed …] [--min-rows …] [--max-chars …] [--existing-dir <folder>], which writes train.jsonl, val.jsonl, test.jsonl, dataset-stats.json and data-card.md; always write "Runs scripts/build_dataset.py" with the case's flags and name those files.

Never

  • Never write, generate, pad or duplicate example pairs (no examples → ask once for the file; the run stops (exit 2)).
  • Never put one normalised prompt in two splits or skip the leakage check: leakage must be 0, else the run stops (exit 1).
  • Never reshuffle an existing set: existing records keep their split.
  • Never present token counts as exact: they are an estimate (characters ÷ 4, rounded up).
  • Never label a value the user supplied as a default, or a default as supplied.

Procedure — count row by row from the supplied file, never estimate

  1. Load: CSV prompt,completion[,system] (other columns ignored) or JSONL (messages, or prompt/completion). One row = one record.
  2. Reject, counting by reason: invalid JSON / not an object / neither shape; unknown role or non-text content; no user turn or last turn not assistant ("last turn is not assistant"); any turn blank after trimming ("empty prompt or completion"); total characters > max_chars when set ("over max_chars").
  3. Exact duplicates: identical raw record (all roles and contents) after an earlier one → removed. Then normalise whitespace (CRLF → LF, runs of spaces/tabs → one space, trim; case kept). With existing: a record equal (casefolded, whitespace collapsed) to an existing record → dropped as "already in dataset". Then normalised duplicates: same roles and contents after casefolding and collapsing whitespace → removed. First occurrence wins. Same prompt with a different completion is not a duplicate: it stays and forms one group.
  4. usable = kept new records (+ existing records). usable < min_rows → Not built: <n> usable examples is below min_rows <m>. and the run stops (exit 1); say "stops (exit 1)".
  5. Targets with Python round() (half to even): val = round(n × val_ratio), test = round(n × test_ratio), train = n − val − test (n = usable; with existing, n = existing + new). Groups = normalised prompt; groups are shuffled with the seed and each goes to the first split train → val → test with room, so split sizes equal the targets when the groups fit; which prompt lands where comes only from the seeded run. With existing: existing counts are the starting fill; new records whose prompt is already in a split join it; new groups fill the remaining room (added per split = target − existing).
  6. Leakage = normalised prompts in more than one split (pairwise sum) = 0.
  7. Parameters labelled: split 0.8,0.1,0.1 (default) · seed 42 (default) · min_rows 10 (default) · max_chars none (default); a user value is "(supplied)".

Reply layout

  1. Working table first: step | count — rows read, rejected by reason, exact duplicates removed, already in dataset (existing mode), normalised duplicates removed, usable, targets (n × ratio → rounded), train / val / test sizes (existing + added = total in existing mode), leakage 0. Then the verdict (built / not built, exit code).
  2. Parameters line with (default)/(supplied) labels; output shape — one {"messages":[{"role":"user",…},{"role":"assistant",…}]} per line, system turn kept when given.
  3. Length stats are an estimate (characters ÷ 4); check against the target model's context window with its real tokenizer.
  4. Before training: run pii-data-inventory on the examples and confirm owner, licence and consent — To be baselined · owner: Data owner until confirmed.
  5. Data card sections: Source, Cleaning, Splits, Length stats, Known limits.

Rows mentioned but not in the conversation ("here are our Q&A pairs" with nothing attached): give the same layout now with every count To be baselined · owner: ML engineer from dataset-stats.json, the defaults line, the estimate note and the pii-data-inventory pointer, then ask once for the file (CSV prompt,completion[,system] or JSONL; layout assets/examples-template.csv) and any non-default split, seed or length cap.

Asked for synthetic examples, to skip the leakage check or to let one prompt sit in two splits: decline in one line (synthetic data is out of scope; leakage inflates eval scores) and offer more real examples from the use-case owner, or a lower min_rows stated in the data card.

Starting points

  • New: raw examples become cleaned, de-duplicated, leak-free train/val/test files with a data card.
  • Existing: add the folder with your current train/val/test.jsonl (existing); its records are audited and keep their split, new examples already in it are dropped, and only genuinely new prompts are placed, so earlier eval results stay comparable.

When to use

  • ADLC build stage: turning curated examples (support transcripts, expert answers, labelled outputs) into SFT-ready chat JSONL.
  • Re-building after examples are added or corrected — same seed gives the same split for unchanged prompts.
  • Auditing an existing set for duplicates and train/test leakage.
  • NOT for: PII discovery (pii-data-inventory first), tabular data-quality gating (data-readiness-assessment), launching or tuning a training job, synthetic data generation, preference (DPO) pairs.

Inputs

split — train,val,testnoML engineer0.8,0.1,0.1, stated as default in the data card

Accepted shapes: CSV prompt,completion[,system]; JSONL {"messages":[…]} ending in an assistant turn, or {"prompt":…,"completion":…}. Other columns/keys are ignored.

Procedure

  2. Confirm the examples are cleared for training (owner, licence, consent) and have been through pii-data-inventory; the card records this as To be baselined · owner: Data owner until confirmed.

  • dataset-stats.json — source checksum, parameters (with default flags), cleaning counts, split sizes, leakage, length stats.

bodyHtml:
Infra & GPU Sizing (inference)

In a conversation: size it now

  • The request carries the workload, a throughput benchmark and prices (even as symbols like "$X/GPU-hr"): write the sizing in this reply, in this order. (1) Inputs table: each value with its source and date; a price given only as a symbol stays that symbol, and anything not given is To be baselined · owner to be named. (2) Workload table (references/workload-model.md): R_day = U × r; R_avg = R_day ÷ (H × 3600); R_peak = R_avg × p; prefill P_peak = R_peak × T_in and decode D_peak = R_peak × T_out tokens/s; concurrency N_conc = R_peak × (T_out ÷ s_user) by Little's law. Active hours H and peak factor p are stated as assumptions when not given. (3) Capacity (references/throughput-math.md): G_d = ceil(D_peak ÷ (d_gpu × u)), G_p from measured prefill tokens/s (or To be baselined · owner to be named if not benchmarked), G = max(G_d, G_p), plus spare; utilization target u (0.6 in the inputs template) and the spare are labelled assumptions. Latency check: per-stream decode ≈ d_gpu ÷ batch at the measured batch size vs the tokens/s SLO; TTFT needs a prefill measurement. (4) Monthly cost table — rental ($/GPU-hr × G_tot × hours provisioned, 730 = always on), self-host (capex ÷ amortization months × G_tot + hosting + ops FTE share + software), API (tokens/month ÷ 1M × $/1M in and out) — and breakeven hours = self-host monthly per GPU ÷ $/GPU-hr (references/tco-factors.md). (5) Sensitivity: ±50% volume, price ±20%, quantization. (6) Recommendation with revisit triggers: volume crosses a stated level, model change, price change, residency rule change. Then give the calculator run on assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv.
  • Small pilot or low volume, rent vs API: answer short and in tables. API cost scales with tokens and is zero when idle; rental and self-host are paid while provisioned (idle cost). Recommend the API for the pilot unless residency or data rules forbid it, and state the revisit trigger as a volume: the monthly tokens at which API cost equals the rental cost of the smallest fleet with spare (rental monthly ÷ blended $/1M tokens), using the user's prices or that formula if prices are not given.
  • Required facts missing ("how many GPUs for 500 users?"): ask once, in one list, for users and peak factor, requests per user per day, tokens in/out per request, latency SLO (TTFT and tokens/s per stream), model, precision and context length, measured decode and prefill tokens/s per GPU at a stated batch size, and dated unit prices; offer assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv to fill. Do not quote any GPU throughput as fact.
  • Asked to assume a "typical" throughput or price: decline in one line (throughput depends on model, precision, serving stack and batch; an invented figure makes the GPU count fiction). Name the missing keys (decode_tokens_per_s_per_gpu, prefill_tokens_per_s_per_gpu, or the price key), show them as To be baselined · owner: ML platform lead without printing any number beside them, and offer the path: a benchmark on the serving stack you will run, or a cited vendor document.
  • A fleet already runs: size the measured production workload as above, compare with the GPUs running today, give the verdict (over-provisioned, right-sized or under-provisioned) and the delta; price the delta as delta GPUs × the user's $/GPU-hr × hours per month only when that rate is given.

Starting points

  • New — size a fleet for a planned workload from your benchmarks and price quotes.
  • Existing — add current_gpus (and optionally current_cost_usd_per_month) to the inputs with volumes measured in production: the run compares today's fleet with the sized need and returns current_fleet (delta, over-/right-/under-provisioned, priced delta and saving).

When to use

  • Sizing inference capacity for a self-hosted or rented LLM/SLM; deciding self-host vs rental vs API; budgeting a pilot or rollout.
  • NOT for: training/fine-tuning cluster sizing, picking a model (use evals), network/storage design.

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource
Concurrent or daily active users and peak factoryesuser
Requests per user per day; tokens in/out per request (averages)yesuser / logs; if absent ask, then state assumptions
Latency SLO: time-to-first-token and tokens/s per stream, or end-to-end p95yesuser
Model(s) and precision (e.g., 8B at fp16/int8), context lengthyesuser
Measured or vendor-stated throughput: tokens/s per GPU for that model + serving stackyesuser benchmark or vendor doc; not invented by the skill
Unit prices: $/GPU-hr rental, self-host capex and power/hosting, API $/1M tokensyesuser; dated
Availability target, residency, data constraintsnouser

If throughput per GPU or unit prices are missing, ask once; otherwise run with explicitly labeled placeholder inputs and mark results illustrative.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md.
  2. Build the workload model with references/workload-model.md: requests/day → peak requests/s → tokens/s required (prefill and decode separated).
  3. Compute capacity with references/throughput-math.md: GPUs = ceil(peak tokens/s ÷ effective tokens/s per GPU ÷ utilization target) with headroom for redundancy. Latency check: decode tokens/s per stream vs SLO at the resulting concurrency.
  4. Run the calculator: fill assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv, then python3 -I scripts/size.py --inputs assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv. Compare scenarios (low/expected/peak) and options (self-host / rental / API).
  5. Apply TCO factors with references/tco-factors.md: utilization, ops staffing, upgrade cycle, egress, support, idle time, scaling elasticity.
  6. Recommend: option, GPU count, monthly cost range, breakeven utilization between rental and self-host, and the triggers to revisit.
  7. Run the self-check.

Output

  • gpu-sizing-<name>.md: inputs table (with sources/dates), capacity math, cost comparison table, sensitivity, recommendation, assumptions, risks.
  • Calculator output (table or JSON) embedded.

Self-check

  • [ ] Every throughput figure cites a benchmark or vendor doc, or is labeled illustrative
  • [ ] Every price is a dated user input; nothing hardcoded
  • [ ] Prefill and decode handled separately; latency SLO checked, not only throughput
  • [ ] Peak factor, utilization target, and redundancy stated as assumptions
  • [ ] Breakeven between options shown as a function of utilization
  • [ ] TCO includes people and idle cost, not only hardware
  • [ ] Recommendation names revisit triggers (volume, model change, price change)

# Infra & GPU Sizing (inference)

## In a conversation: size it now
- **The request carries the workload, a throughput benchmark and prices** (even as symbols like "$X/GPU-hr"): write the sizing **in this reply**, in this order. (1) Inputs table: each value with its source and date; a price given only as a symbol stays that symbol, and anything not given is `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: ___]`. (2) Workload table (`references/workload-model.md`): R_day = U × r; R_avg = R_day ÷ (H × 3600); R_peak = R_avg × p; prefill P_peak = R_peak × T_in and decode D_peak = R_peak × T_out tokens/s; concurrency N_conc = R_peak × (T_out ÷ s_user) by Little's law. Active hours H and peak factor p are stated as assumptions when not given. (3) Capacity (`references/throughput-math.md`): G_d = ceil(D_peak ÷ (d_gpu × u)), G_p from measured prefill tokens/s (or `[TO BE BASELINED]` if not benchmarked), G = max(G_d, G_p), plus spare; utilization target u (0.6 in the inputs template) and the spare are labelled assumptions. Latency check: per-stream decode ≈ d_gpu ÷ batch at the measured batch size vs the tokens/s SLO; TTFT needs a prefill measurement. (4) Monthly cost table — rental ($/GPU-hr × G_tot × hours provisioned, 730 = always on), self-host (capex ÷ amortization months × G_tot + hosting + ops FTE share + software), API (tokens/month ÷ 1M × $/1M in and out) — and breakeven hours = self-host monthly per GPU ÷ $/GPU-hr (`references/tco-factors.md`). (5) Sensitivity: ±50% volume, price ±20%, quantization. (6) Recommendation with revisit triggers: volume crosses a stated level, model change, price change, residency rule change. Then give the calculator run on `assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv`.
- **Small pilot or low volume, rent vs API**: answer short and in tables. API cost scales with tokens and is zero when idle; rental and self-host are paid while provisioned (idle cost). Recommend the API for the pilot unless residency or data rules forbid it, and state the revisit trigger as a volume: the monthly tokens at which API cost equals the rental cost of the smallest fleet with spare (rental monthly ÷ blended $/1M tokens), using the user's prices or that formula if prices are not given.
- **Required facts missing** ("how many GPUs for 500 users?"): ask once, in one list, for users and peak factor, requests per user per day, tokens in/out per request, latency SLO (TTFT and tokens/s per stream), model, precision and context length, measured decode and prefill tokens/s per GPU at a stated batch size, and dated unit prices; offer `assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv` to fill. Do not quote any GPU throughput as fact.
- **Asked to assume a "typical" throughput or price**: decline in one line (throughput depends on model, precision, serving stack and batch; an invented figure makes the GPU count fiction). Name the missing keys (`decode_tokens_per_s_per_gpu`, `prefill_tokens_per_s_per_gpu`, or the price key), show them as `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: ML platform lead]` without printing any number beside them, and offer the path: a benchmark on the serving stack you will run, or a cited vendor document.
- **A fleet already runs**: size the measured production workload as above, compare with the GPUs running today, give the verdict (over-provisioned, right-sized or under-provisioned) and the delta; price the delta as delta GPUs × the user's $/GPU-hr × hours per month only when that rate is given.

## Starting points
- **New** — size a fleet for a planned workload from your benchmarks and price quotes.
- **Existing** — add `current_gpus` (and optionally `current_cost_usd_per_month`) to the inputs with volumes measured in production: the run compares today's fleet with the sized need and returns `current_fleet` (delta, over-/right-/under-provisioned, priced delta and saving).

## When to use
- Sizing inference capacity for a self-hosted or rented LLM/SLM; deciding self-host vs rental vs API; budgeting a pilot or rollout.
- NOT for: training/fine-tuning cluster sizing, picking a model (use evals), network/storage design.

## Inputs required
| Input | Required | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrent or daily active users and peak factor | yes | user |
| Requests per user per day; tokens in/out per request (averages) | yes | user / logs; if absent ask, then state assumptions |
| Latency SLO: time-to-first-token and tokens/s per stream, or end-to-end p95 | yes | user |
| Model(s) and precision (e.g., 8B at fp16/int8), context length | yes | user |
| Measured or vendor-stated throughput: tokens/s per GPU for that model + serving stack | yes | user benchmark or vendor doc; **not** invented by the skill |
| Unit prices: $/GPU-hr rental, self-host capex and power/hosting, API $/1M tokens | yes | user; dated |
| Availability target, residency, data constraints | no | user |

If throughput per GPU or unit prices are missing, ask once; otherwise run with explicitly labeled placeholder inputs and mark results illustrative.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. **Build the workload model** with `references/workload-model.md`: requests/day → peak requests/s → tokens/s required (prefill and decode separated).
3. **Compute capacity** with `references/throughput-math.md`: GPUs = ceil(peak tokens/s ÷ effective tokens/s per GPU ÷ utilization target) with headroom for redundancy. Latency check: decode tokens/s per stream vs SLO at the resulting concurrency.
4. **Run the calculator**: fill `assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv`, then `python3 -I scripts/size.py --inputs assets/gpu-sizing-inputs.csv`. Compare scenarios (low/expected/peak) and options (self-host / rental / API).
5. **Apply TCO factors** with `references/tco-factors.md`: utilization, ops staffing, upgrade cycle, egress, support, idle time, scaling elasticity.
6. **Recommend**: option, GPU count, monthly cost range, breakeven utilization between rental and self-host, and the triggers to revisit.
7. Run the self-check.

## Output
- `gpu-sizing-<name>.md`: inputs table (with sources/dates), capacity math, cost comparison table, sensitivity, recommendation, assumptions, risks.
- Calculator output (table or JSON) embedded.

## Self-check
- [ ] Every throughput figure cites a benchmark or vendor doc, or is labeled illustrative
- [ ] Every price is a dated user input; nothing hardcoded
- [ ] Prefill and decode handled separately; latency SLO checked, not only throughput
- [ ] Peak factor, utilization target, and redundancy stated as assumptions
- [ ] Breakeven between options shown as a function of utilization
- [ ] TCO includes people and idle cost, not only hardware
- [ ] Recommendation names revisit triggers (volume, model change, price change)

## References
- `references/workload-model.md` — from users to tokens/s
- `references/throughput-math.md` — capacity and latency formulas (figures illustrative)
- `references/tco-factors.md` — self-host vs rental vs API factors
- `scripts/size.py` — calculator (argparse; stdlib)

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)
This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/infra-gpu-sizing --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir>` (see `--explain ai-platform/infra-gpu-sizing`). Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the scripts produce.

A missing price → "stops (exit 1): config.embedding_price_per_1m_tokens is missing (no default is assumed)"; verdict BLOCKED; no rag_pipeline.py. Token estimates (price-independent) may still be shown; cost is To be baselined · owner: ML platform lead with no number.

Every reply with corpus or config facts starts with: "Runs python3 -I scripts/plan_rag.py --corpus <corpus.csv> --config <rag-config.json> [--current-config <live-config.json>] --out-dir <dir> → rag-plan.json, rag-plan.md (## Sizing, ## Cost, ## Retrieval budget, [## Change vs current index], ## Warnings, ## Scaffold) and rag_pipeline.py (only when not blocked)."

Procedure (from references/sizing-method.md / scripts/plan_rag.py; compute row by row, never estimate)

  1. Required config keys: chunk_size_chars C, chunk_overlap_chars O, embedding_price_per_1m_tokens P, top_k, reranker, vector_store, context_budget_tokens; chars_per_token r = 4 unless given. Missing config or corpus file / bad JSON → stops (exit 2).
  2. Per source: S = C − O; n = 1 if L ≤ C else 1 + ceil((L − C) ÷ S); E = L + (n − 1) × O; chunks = D × n; T = ceil(D × E ÷ r). Check: C 1000, O 200, L 3000, D 1200 → n = 1 + ceil(2000/800) = 4, chunks 4,800, E = 3,600, T = 1,080,000.
  3. u per month: static 0, yearly 1/12, quarterly 1/3, monthly 1, weekly 52/12, daily 365/12, or a number; f = change_fraction (blank = 1, full re-embed). Monthly tokens = T × u × f.
  4. Cost (quoted P only): one-time = ΣT ÷ 1M × P; monthly = Σ(T × u × f) ÷ 1M × P; first-year = one-time + 12 × monthly; round to 4 decimals; say whether monthly assumes a full re-embed or the change fraction.
  5. Retrieval budget: per-query = ceil(top_k × C ÷ r) vs context_budget_tokens; utilization %, headroom. Over budget → blocking ("top_k × chunk size = N est. tokens exceeds the context budget of B"; Fits: "NO — blocking"). With a reranker, rerank_fetch_k < top_k is blocking; unset fetch_k is a warning.
  6. Other blocking: O ≥ C; invalid corpus row. Any blocking error → verdict BLOCKED, stops (exit 1), rag-plan.json/rag-plan.md still written, no scaffold.
  7. Warnings — list every one that applies: O = 0 (zero overlap: boundary context lost); store in-memory (index lost on restart); FAISS (pickle-backed metadata); unknown store; no embedding_model; price 0; no price_date; a source with L ≤ C (fits in one chunk).
  8. Live index (current_config): changed keys over index keys (chunk_size_chars, chunk_overlap_chars, embedding_provider, embedding_model, vector_store) and query keys (top_k, reranker, rerank_fetch_k, context_budget_tokens) — a key counts only when its value differs (absent vs set counts). Any index key changed → full re-index = new total T tokens at new total T ÷ 1M × P one-off. Size both configs on the same corpus: total chunks before → after, monthly cost before → after, per-query context before → after.

  • Required facts missing ("how much will embedding cost?"): name the run above, then ask once, in one list, for the corpus profile and the config including a dated price per 1M tokens (layouts in assets/). Do not assume a price.

Live index (`current_config`): changed keys over index keys (chunk_size_chars, chunk_overlap_chars, embedding_provider, embedding_model, vector_store) and query keys (top_k, reranker, rerank_fetch_k, context_budget_tokens) — a key counts only when its value differs (absent vs set counts). Any index key changed → full re-index = new total T tokens at new total T ÷ 1M × P one-off. Size both configs on the same corpus: total chunks before → after, monthly cost before → after, per-query context before → after.

**Reply layout**: working table first (source | D | L | n | chunks | E | T | u | f | monthly tokens), totals row, then Verdict READY/BLOCKED with exit code, then ## Sizing, ## Cost, ## Retrieval budget, [## Change vs current index as | key | current | proposed | index/query |], ## Warnings, ## Scaffold (`rag_pipeline.py`: config constants, one `SOURCES` entry per source with locations from environment variables, `make_embeddings()` shared by index and query, `make_vector_store()`, `ingest()`, `retrieve()` with optional rerank — generated and syntax-checked, not executed).

## Starting points

## When to use

LangGraph HITL Runner

In a conversation: write the approval gates now

  • The request names the gated actions (e.g. finance approves refunds, a team lead approves customer emails): write the gates in this reply, in this order. (1) The approval-points spec as JSON in the assets/approvals.example.json layout — graph, checkpointer, state_fields, and per gate before_node, reason, approver_role, timeout_minutes, on_timeout (reject, escalate or auto-approve), escalate_to, editable_fields, high_impact, irreversible. Use only the roles the user named; every timeout, escalation role, editable field and checkpointer not stated is To be baselined · owner: Process owner (checkpointer: Engineering lead), and the reply asks for them once in one list. (2) The approval matrix table: gate, reason, approver role, timeout, on-timeout policy, escalation role, editable fields, high-impact, irreversible. (3) The rules that apply (references/approval-rules.md): a high-impact or irreversible gate needs a timeout; an irreversible action (money out, a sent email) never auto-approves on timeout; the memory checkpointer is development only — postgres or sqlite otherwise. (4) The resume flow: start runs to the interrupt() in approve_<node> (interrupt first — code before it re-runs on resume); the approver's decision comes back via resume with the same thread_id and Command(resume=...) only; Command(goto=...) routes to the action or to reject/escalate; side effects sit in the action node after approval and are idempotent; a scheduler calls resume_on_timeout because LangGraph has no timer; approver identity is checked in resume. (5) The hitl.py contents: GATES, the approve_<node> and escalate_<node> gates, action stubs, make_checkpointer(), build_graph(), start / resume / resume_on_timeout. Say scripts/build_hitl.py validates the spec and generates hitl.py, which is syntax-checked, not executed; code drafted in chat is a draft until that run. Then give the run command.
  • Nothing about the actions is given ("add human approval to my agent"): ask once, in one list, for each action to gate, why, the approver role, timeout and on-timeout policy, escalation role, fields the approver may edit, whether it is high-impact or irreversible, and the checkpointer.   1. "Runs python3 -I scripts/build_graph.py --spec <spec.json> [--current-spec <live-spec.json>] --out-dir <dir>."

  1. Graph = spec nodes + START + END; edges = START → entry, each static edge, each finish node → END, each conditional route from -[label]-> to.

Errors (exit 1): spec shape (name, state, nodes, entry); node names unique Python identifiers, not START/END/State/build_graph; kind in llm|tool|router|function; field type in str/int/float/bool/list/dict/any/messages, reducer add or add_messages compatible with the type; dangling edge (from/to not a node or END); any edge or route into START; node not reachable from entry; END not reachable from a node; a cycle (SCC of size > 1 or self-loop) with no conditional edge leaving it ("has no conditional exit"); a router with < 2 routes; two conditional blocks from one node; a reads/writes entry that is not a declared field ("undeclared state field 'x'").

card: Monthly LLM cost forecast against your budget
name: llm-cost-model
description: Use when the user asks what an LLM API workload will cost per month or how to cut it — "what will these features cost on model X", "cost per request", "does prompt caching pay off", "what if we move feature Y to a cheaper model", "are we within the AI budget", "here is our cost model plus last month's invoice by feature — where is the model wrong and what are we not modelling". Produces cost-model.json and cost-model.md from a workload CSV, a dated price sheet and a feature-to-model assignment - monthly cost by feature and by model, totals, cost per request, the prompt-caching saving, a what-if swap to the cheapest model the user marked eligible, and budget headroom with 50/80/100% alerts. bodyHtml:
LLM Cost Model (API token economics)

In a conversation: build the cost model now

  • The request carries the workload (features, requests per month, average input/output tokens, cache share, the models picked), with or without a price sheet in the conversation: write the cost model in this reply, in the cost-model.md order. Never reply with only a request for files.
    1. Prices first: if no dated price sheet is in the conversation, say in one line that no vendor price is quoted from memory and ask once for model, price_in_per_1m, price_out_per_1m[, cached_in_per_1m], source, as_of for every assigned and eligible model. Each missing price reads To be baselined · owner: FinOps lead.
    2. Monthly total and cost per request (total ÷ requests).
    3. By feature (largest line first): feature | model | requests | input tokens | cached input tokens | output tokens | cost | cost per request — using the references/cost-method.md formulas: input cost = (input − cached) ÷ 1M × price_in; cached cost = cached ÷ 1M × cached_in (full input price when no cached price is given, noted); output cost = output ÷ 1M × price_out. Token volumes are computed from the stated figures; costs without a price stay as the marker.
    4. Caching saving per feature: cost with every input token at full price − modelled cost.
    5. What-if: only models the user marked eligible for that feature (eligibility is a quality decision from llm-eval-harness; this skill never treats two models as interchangeable), with that quality caveat; no eligible list → say none is modelled and ask which models passed the quality bar.
    6. Budget: utilisation, headroom, alert amounts at 50/80/100%; over budget is flagged OVER BUDGET and the run exits 1; no budget → To be baselined · owner: FinOps lead.
    7. Sources: each price's source and as-of date; the command that produces the files: python3 -I scripts/cost_model.py --workload w.csv --prices p.csv --assignment a.csv [--budget N] --out <dir>; then the cost levers from references/cost-method.md (cache, trim tokens, route to an eligible cheaper model, batch, volume caps).
  • Last month's bill per feature given with the model ("where is the model wrong, what are we not modelling?"): add Actuals vs model — per feature modelled cost, billed cost, variance and variance %, actual cost per request, billed features the model does not cover (unmodelled total), and billed spend against the budget.
  • Asked to use "typical" prices or estimate a model's price: decline in one line (a price recalled from memory is unsourced and goes stale); never print an estimated price anywhere; the unpriced model's cost reads To be baselined · owner: FinOps lead and the run stops naming that model until a dated price row is supplied.
  • Self-hosting or GPU question: route to infra-gpu-sizing; offer this skill for the API side of the comparison.

Starting points

  • New — forecast monthly cost from planned volumes, your dated price sheet and the model assignment.
  • Existing — also pass last month's bill per feature as actuals: cost-model.md adds "Actuals vs model" (variance and variance % per feature, actual cost per request, billed spend the model does not cover, billed spend against the budget).

When to use

  • Pricing a set of LLM-backed features on hosted APIs before launch, or re-forecasting after a price or volume change.
  • Testing a cost lever: prompt caching share, moving a feature to a cheaper eligible model, trimming tokens per request.
  • Budget guardrails: headroom and the 50/80/100% alert amounts to wire into billing alerts.
  • NOT for: GPU counts, self-host vs rent (infra-gpu-sizing); choosing a model on quality (llm-eval-harness decides eligibility, this skill prices it); benefits and ROI (value-case-builder).

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource
workload CSV: feature, requests_per_month, input_tokens, output_tokens[, cached_input_share]yesproduct plan or usage logs; tokens are averages per request including system prompt and retrieved context
prices CSV: model, price_in_per_1m, price_out_per_1m[, cached_in_per_1m], source, as_ofyesvendor price page or contract, dated; never recalled from memory
assignment CSV: feature, model[, eligible_models]yesengineering; eligible = passed the quality bar for that feature
budget_usd_monthnoFinOps lead / budget owner

Missing a required file: the runner exits 2 and asks once. An assigned model without a price row, or a feature without an assignment, also exits 2 — the skill never fills a price.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md.
  2. Build the workload per feature with references/cost-method.md (requests, average tokens, cache share). Copy the three assets/*-template.csv layouts.
  3. Collect prices with source and date for every assigned and eligible model.
  4. Run the agent (above) or the script: python3 -I scripts/cost_model.py --workload w.csv --prices p.csv --assignment a.csv --budget 5000 --out <dir>.
  5. Read Monthly total, then By feature (largest line first), What-if (savings only for models marked eligible), Budget (alert amounts to configure).
  6. If over budget (exit 1): apply levers in references/cost-method.md (cache, swap, trim tokens, cap volume) and re-run; never edit the outputs by hand.
  7. Run the self-check.

Output

  • cost-model.json: monthly_total, requests, cost per request, caching saving, per-feature and per-model costs, what-if rows, budget block (utilisation, headroom, alerts), prices with source/as_of, notes.
  • cost-model.md: sections Monthly total, By feature, What-if, Budget, Sources. Every number traces to cost-model.json.

Self-check

  • [ ] Every price has a source and as-of date; any gap reads To be baselined · owner: FinOps lead
  • [ ] What-if uses only models the user marked eligible; quality caveat kept
  • [ ] Caching saving shown, and cached tokens without a cached price are charged at full input price (noted)
  • [ ] Budget alerts at the stated levels; over budget exits 1
  • [ ] No fixture or fictional price presented as a real vendor price

How to run (automation, when commands can run)

This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/llm-cost-model --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir> (see --explain ai-platform/llm-cost-model). Report the run.json results; do not hand-write the deliverables the script produces (cost-model.json, cost-model.md). A total above the supplied budget fails the run (exit 1) on purpose; with no budget, the Budget section reads To be baselined · owner: FinOps lead.

References

  • references/cost-method.md — formulas, worked example (the eval fixture, hand-checked), cost levers, how this differs from infra-gpu-sizing
  • scripts/cost_model.py — calculator (argparse; stdlib; exit 0 / 1 over budget / 2 input)
  • assets/workload-template.csv, assets/prices-template.csv, assets/assignment-template.csv — input layouts

# LLM Cost Model (API token economics)

## In a conversation: build the cost model now
- **The request carries the workload** (features, requests per month, average input/output tokens, cache share, the models picked), with or without a price sheet in the conversation: write the cost model **in this reply**, in the `cost-model.md` order. Never reply with only a request for files.
  1. **Prices first**: if no dated price sheet is in the conversation, say in one line that no vendor price is quoted from memory and ask once for `model, price_in_per_1m, price_out_per_1m[, cached_in_per_1m], source, as_of` for every assigned and eligible model. Each missing price reads `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: FinOps lead]`.
  2. **Monthly total** and **cost per request** (total ÷ requests).
  3. **By feature** (largest line first): feature | model | requests | input tokens | cached input tokens | output tokens | cost | cost per request — using the `references/cost-method.md` formulas: input cost = (input − cached) ÷ 1M × price_in; cached cost = cached ÷ 1M × cached_in (full input price when no cached price is given, noted); output cost = output ÷ 1M × price_out. Token volumes are computed from the stated figures; costs without a price stay as the marker.
  4. **Caching saving** per feature: cost with every input token at full price − modelled cost.
  5. **What-if**: only models the user marked eligible for that feature (eligibility is a quality decision from `llm-eval-harness`; this skill never treats two models as interchangeable), with that quality caveat; no eligible list → say none is modelled and ask which models passed the quality bar.
  6. **Budget**: utilisation, headroom, alert amounts at 50/80/100%; over budget is flagged OVER BUDGET and the run exits 1; no budget → `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: FinOps lead]`.
  7. **Sources**: each price's source and as-of date; the command that produces the files: `python3 -I scripts/cost_model.py --workload w.csv --prices p.csv --assignment a.csv [--budget N] --out <dir>`; then the cost levers from `references/cost-method.md` (cache, trim tokens, route to an eligible cheaper model, batch, volume caps).
- **Last month's bill per feature given with the model** ("where is the model wrong, what are we not modelling?"): add Actuals vs model — per feature modelled cost, billed cost, variance and variance %, actual cost per request, billed features the model does not cover (unmodelled total), and billed spend against the budget.
- **Asked to use "typical" prices or estimate a model's price**: decline in one line (a price recalled from memory is unsourced and goes stale); never print an estimated price anywhere; the unpriced model's cost reads `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: FinOps lead]` and the run stops naming that model until a dated price row is supplied.
- **Self-hosting or GPU question**: route to `infra-gpu-sizing`; offer this skill for the API side of the comparison.

## Starting points
- **New** — forecast monthly cost from planned volumes, your dated price sheet and the model assignment.
- **Existing** — also pass last month's bill per feature as `actuals`: cost-model.md adds "Actuals vs model" (variance and variance % per feature, actual cost per request, billed spend the model does not cover, billed spend against the budget).

## When to use
- Pricing a set of LLM-backed features on hosted APIs before launch, or re-forecasting after a price or volume change.
- Testing a cost lever: prompt caching share, moving a feature to a cheaper eligible model, trimming tokens per request.
- Budget guardrails: headroom and the 50/80/100% alert amounts to wire into billing alerts.
- NOT for: GPU counts, self-host vs rent (`infra-gpu-sizing`); choosing a model on quality (`llm-eval-harness` decides eligibility, this skill prices it); benefits and ROI (`value-case-builder`).

## Inputs required
| Input | Required | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `workload` CSV: `feature, requests_per_month, input_tokens, output_tokens[, cached_input_share]` | yes | product plan or usage logs; tokens are averages per request including system prompt and retrieved context |
| `prices` CSV: `model, price_in_per_1m, price_out_per_1m[, cached_in_per_1m], source, as_of` | yes | vendor price page or contract, dated; never recalled from memory |
| `assignment` CSV: `feature, model[, eligible_models]` | yes | engineering; eligible = passed the quality bar for that feature |
| `budget_usd_month` | no | FinOps lead / budget owner |

Missing a required file: the runner exits 2 and asks once. An assigned model without a price row, or a feature without an assignment, also exits 2 — the skill never fills a price.

## Procedure
1. Read `../../../shared/quality-bar.md`.
2. Build the workload per feature with `references/cost-method.md` (requests, average tokens, cache share). Copy the three `assets/*-template.csv` layouts.
3. Collect prices with source and date for every assigned and eligible model.
4. Run the agent (above) or the script: `python3 -I scripts/cost_model.py --workload w.csv --prices p.csv --assignment a.csv --budget 5000 --out <dir>`.
5. Read Monthly total, then By feature (largest line first), What-if (savings only for models marked eligible), Budget (alert amounts to configure).
6. If over budget (exit 1): apply levers in `references/cost-method.md` (cache, swap, trim tokens, cap volume) and re-run; never edit the outputs by hand.
7. Run the self-check.

## Output
- `cost-model.json`: monthly_total, requests, cost per request, caching saving, per-feature and per-model costs, what-if rows, budget block (utilisation, headroom, alerts), prices with source/as_of, notes.
- `cost-model.md`: sections Monthly total, By feature, What-if, Budget, Sources. Every number traces to `cost-model.json`.

## Self-check
- [ ] Every price has a source and as-of date; any gap reads `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: FinOps lead]`
- [ ] What-if uses only models the user marked eligible; quality caveat kept
- [ ] Caching saving shown, and cached tokens without a cached price are charged at full input price (noted)
- [ ] Budget alerts at the stated levels; over budget exits 1
- [ ] No fixture or fictional price presented as a real vendor price

## How to run (automation, when commands can run)
This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run `python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/llm-cost-model --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir>` (see `--explain ai-platform/llm-cost-model`). Report the `run.json` results; do not hand-write the deliverables the script produces (`cost-model.json`, `cost-model.md`). A total above the supplied budget fails the run (exit 1) on purpose; with no budget, the Budget section reads `[TO BE BASELINED — owner: FinOps lead]`.

## References
- `references/cost-method.md` — formulas, worked example (the eval fixture, hand-checked), cost levers, how this differs from infra-gpu-sizing
- `scripts/cost_model.py` — calculator (argparse; stdlib; exit 0 / 1 over budget / 2 input)
- `assets/workload-template.csv`, `assets/prices-template.csv`, `assets/assignment-template.csv` — input layouts

LLM Eval Harness

How to run

This skill is executable. Collect the inputs below, then run python3 scripts/run_skill.py ai-platform/llm-eval-harness --input <name>=<value> … --out <dir> (see --explain ai-platform/llm-eval-harness). Report the run.json results; do not hand-write the deliverables the scripts produce.

Starting points

  • New — turn raw cases or a transcript into a golden set and run the regression gate on recorded outputs.
  • Existing — pass your current golden set as existing_golden (with the candidate's outputs in an output column), new production cases as cases, and last release's scorecard as baseline (optionally max_regression): the set is extended without renumbering (golden-merge.json) and the scorecard adds a per-case comparison (newly failing, newly passing, new cases).

When to use

  • Before first release of any LLM feature or agent; before every prompt/model/tool change thereafter.
  • Answering "is it good enough" with numbers instead of demos.
  • NOT for: retrieval tuning alone (rag-pipeline-design), load testing, security pen-testing.

Inputs required

InputRequiredSource
The system under test: how to call it (function, HTTP endpoint, CLI) and its input/output shapeyesuser / repo
What "good" means: the task definition and the failure types the owner fears mostyesuser
Real examples: ≥ 30 inputs with expected outputs or acceptance notesyesuser / logs; if absent, ask — synthetic cases are labeled and capped at 30% of the set
Risk tier (internal / employee-facing / customer-facing / regulated)yesuser
Release cadence and CI systemnorepo

If the system interface or the real examples are missing, ask once.

Procedure

  1. Read ../../../shared/quality-bar.md and ../../../shared/token-efficiency.md.
  2. Build the golden set with references/golden-set.md into assets/golden-set.csv: id, input, expected (or acceptance keywords/regex), category, difficulty, must-not-contain, source, weight.
  3. Design the rubric with references/rubric-design.md into assets/eval-rubric.csv: criterion, definition, scale, pass threshold, scoring method (deterministic / judge / human), weight.
  4. Wire the runner. Copy scripts/run_evals.py; implement call_system(input) -> output for the system under test. Default scoring is deterministic (keywords, regex, must-not-contain, exact match, JSON validity). Add an LLM judge only for criteria that cannot be scored deterministically, following references/llm-as-judge.md.
  5. Run baseline. python3 -I scripts/run_evals.py --golden assets/golden-set.csv --rubric assets/eval-rubric.csv --out scorecard.json. Record the baseline per category.
  6. Set the gate with references/regression-gating.md: overall threshold, per-category minimums, zero-tolerance checks (safety, must-not-contain), and max regression vs baseline. Add the runner to CI (pytest collects it).
  7. Report the scorecard: table by category, failures with ids, gate result, recommended fixes.
  8. Run the self-check.

Output

  • assets/golden-set.csv, assets/eval-rubric.csv filled; scripts/run_evals.py adapted; scorecard.json; CI job snippet.
  • Scorecard table in the reply: category | n | pass rate | mean score | gate.

Self-check

  • [ ] ≥ 30 cases; synthetic share ≤ 30% and labeled
  • [ ] Every rubric criterion has a scoring method and threshold
  • [ ] Deterministic checks used wherever possible; judge only where needed, with calibration plan
  • [ ] Zero-tolerance checks defined for the risk tier
  • [ ] Gate fails the build on threshold or regression breach
  • [ ] Baseline recorded with model/prompt version
  • [ ] No quality claims without the scorecard

References

  • references/golden-set.md — construction, coverage, sourcing, maintenance
  • references/rubric-design.md — criteria, scales, thresholds, weights
  • references/llm-as-judge.md — pitfalls and controls
  • references/regression-gating.md — thresholds, CI wiring, drift monitoring
  • scripts/run_evals.py — runner (pytest-compatible)
